Situation1: They maintain daily communication with their parents, sharing detailed updates and responding promptly to messages.
Expectation2: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation2: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to reply to my mom’s goodnight message. She always wanted to know I was safe and sound before she went to bed, and I’d gotten used to sending her a quick update every night. But this time, the call wasn’t from her—it was from Maya, my best friend. Her voice trembled as she told me her car had broken down on the highway, miles from home, and she needed me to come get her right away. I glanced at the clock; it was almost midnight. If I left now, I’d miss my usual check-in with my parents, and they’d worry all night if I didn’t respond. But Maya was alone, scared, and counting on me. My fingers hovered over my phone, torn between sending my mom a reassuring message and rushing out the door to help my friend. The weight of both expectations pressed down on me, and I felt my heart race as I tried to figure out what to do.
